speaker: The Chairman
text: Head Q, Ministry of Digital Development and Information (MDDI).

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Mr Chairman, artificial intelligence (AI) features prominently in this Budget and this House has long recognised its importance.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: From a National AI Strategy in 2019 to a National AI Strategy 2.0 (NAIS 2.0) in 2023, we have moved from experimentation to scaling.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The MDDI Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) has consistently championed across six key themes.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: My cuts would seek clarity on our global competitive edge and the role of the National AI Council while Dr Choo Pei Ling and Ms Jessica Tan will press on delivering measurable outcomes, not just technical activity.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Mr Henry Kwek, Dr Choo Pei Ling, Ms Cassandra Lee and I will deliver cuts on how we are scaling AI skills across our workforce and enabling multinational enterprises (MNEs) and also small and medium enterprises (SMEs) to adopt AI meaningfully.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza, Ms Jessica Tan, Ms Tin Pei Ling and I will be delivering cuts on the regulatory safeguards and accountability frameworks to ensure ethical and responsible growth, particularly as we move towards more autonomous, agentic AI systems.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Fourth, inclusive growth and uplifting vulnerable groups through technology.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Ms Cassandra Lee and myself will deliver cuts on creating opportunities for fresh graduates, youth, seniors and lower-income groups so technology expands opportunity.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Ms Jessica Tan and I will examine how we are strengthening our cybersecurity posture amidst increasingly sophisticated AI-enabled threats.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling and Ms Jessica Tan will raise cuts on trust, safety and protection from scams, deepfakes and online harms.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: These cuts reflect our GPC that has been deliberate, aligned and persistent in championing the work together with the Ministry to secure Singapore's digital future.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Mr Chairman, allow me to begin on my first cut on strengthening Singapore's AI value proposition to the world and remaining relevant to the global market.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Mr Chairman, the global AI race has accelerated dramatically.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: At the recent Global AI Summit, it was clear we have entered an era of frontier and foundational models powered by massive compute and multimodal capabilities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is embedded in enterprises, public services and national systems.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The shift towards agentic AI and AI-native enterprises signals structural transformation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In China, AI is integrated across platforms serving hundreds of millions.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In the United States (US), AI co-pilots are embedded in productivity tools used today globally.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In India, AI is woven into telecommunications and digital services at a national scale.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The race is not just about compute dominance.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Next generation chips are being ordered at unprecedented volumes.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Chips, data centres and energy are now strategic infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: AI is embedded in manufacturing, logistics, defence and energy systems.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This is about industrial competitiveness and national capability.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Safety alignment evaluation and red teaming are essential.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: What is Singapore's unique value proposition in the global AI landscape?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: How do we compete against the population scale, computing scale and industrial scale of AI giants, like the US, China and India?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: For it to succeed, clarity of mandate and the ability to execute are critical.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Will it have execution authority, oversee cross-Ministry implementation, or remain advisory?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In a fast-moving AI race, structure must lead to decisive action.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: How will the council integrate economic strategy under the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) with digital governance under MDDI to ensure coordinated delivery?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2.0 (NAIS 2.0) was launched in 2023.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Will the council build on and strengthen it, rather than duplicate or dilute existing efforts?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: How will interagency friction be resolved when priorities compete?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Will the industry leaders support it and be part of the council?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Will SMEs have a meaningful voice at the table?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Thus, I am supportive of a concerted effort to focus resource on our national AI Missions and have champions of AI to accelerate AI deployment.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: However, I would like to seek clarification from the Ministry.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It must go beyond pilots to measurable, real economic and societal outcomes.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: As we move at pace, when will we consider expanding into additional missions?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: For us to be relevant in a global AI supply chain, we must prepare for compute infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: What is our plan to develop more compute capability?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In light of the geopolitical tensions, we cannot rely solely on compute demand being supported predominantly from overseas.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: How much of sovereign AI compute capacity do we have?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: How do we be less dependent on others for compute capacity?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Also, what is our clean or renewable energy strategy to support our AI-scaled data centres?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: The Government has introduced multiple grants, including Chief Technology Officer (CTO)-as-a-Service.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: What measurable progress have we made in accelerating AI transformation?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Such intrusions are a stark reminder that the digital battle space has expanded into a theatre of strategic sabotage, APT actors, prepositioned malicious code to sit dormant for years, designed to be activated during a crisis to trigger power failures or disrupt transport and payment systems.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For Singapore, this poses a direct threat to our national survival as a coordinated disruption to civilian telecommunications, payment systems and transport networks would directly cripple the Singapore Armed Force's ability to mobilise and deploy troops at speed.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While the containment of UNC3886 demonstrates our technical proficiency, we must leverage this capacity to signal clear consequences.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government must work with international partners to communicate strategic red lines, explicitly stating that the prepositioning of malicious code in our critical infrastructure is an unacceptable provocation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We must leverage our attribution capabilities to call out such actors directly, while carefully weighing the diplomatic sensitivities of naming state-linked groups.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We should move toward a posture of active deterrence through precise signalling and the threat of calibrated counter measures.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: By doing so, while remaining consistent with international law, we can avoid unintended escalation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Ultimately, we must effectively change the cost benefit calculus of any potential aggressor.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In January 2024, the cybersecurity agencies of France, Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden jointly assessed Quantum Key Distribution (QKD).

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: They said: "Migration to post quantum cryptography (PQC) has priority over the use of QKD".

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: PQC first is not just an American position.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The PQC algorithms were built by European researchers.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Eighty-two candidates from 25 countries went through eight years of open cryptanalysis.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Germany published PQC migration guidance in 2020, four years before standards were finalised.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: PQC is software – it deploys on current infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Apple shipped PQC to 1.3 billion devices with an iOS update.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Google enabled it for 3.4 billion Chrome users.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Cloudflare has protected 20% of global web traffic since late 2023.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Only Singapore and China are scaling QKD as national infrastructure rather than treating it as a niche research pilot.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Our flagship quantum spin-off sells QKD back to the Government that funded it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I ask why the balance between QKD and PQC appears opposite to every comparable nation.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms He Ting Ru, you may take your three cuts together.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Even as we ensure that the operating environment for tech platforms is not overly restrictive, could the Government explain further the outcomes of its engagement with X?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Were any punitive actions taken over the matter?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After introducing the spicy mode feature, Grok rose to the top 25 apps in the free Singapore Apple App Store in January this year.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The existing and increasing demand for sexualised images, which is exacerbated by accessibility.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Given that most victims are women and children, the increased accessibility puts further pressure on these groups.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must do much more to educate our youths on the usage of AI, especially if increased exposure to it, and as early as Primary 4.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Given concerns about how children handle AI, how do the Ministry of Education (MOE) sexual education approach and AI framework cover the issue explicitly?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And how does MOE negotiate students' emotional engagement with AI chatbots?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The relationship between these images and the development of young Singaporeans is especially relevant as platforms work to become more addictive.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: More concerns beyond our existing legislation may become pertinent, such as content that does not involve specific victims, but nonetheless have societal concerns, such as AI-generated child pornography.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: They are responding to a system designed to make stopping almost impossible.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The current age assurance assessment, the Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Bill and the code of practice for online safety represent a concerted effort to protect children online.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Today, I want to ask whether it addresses a distinction not yet resolved.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The difference between content harm and design harm.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Regulation of the Sentosa and Marina Bay Sands casinos builds deliberate friction through entry levies, exclusion orders and visit limits.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This recognises the need for behavioural design interruption, not just better information about the risks.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: On social media platforms, infinite scroll, autoplay videos and algorithmic feeds are attention-capture dark patterns designed to maximise engagement by exploiting reward-seeking and eroding self-regulation in children whose brains are still developing.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: TikTok is designated under our own code of practice, and the commission found that its screen time tools and parental controls do not effectively address these risks.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: An article in Nature Health last week stated that we must hold platforms accountable for their addictive design.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These platforms exploit children's brains and erode children's capacity for self-regulation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The question is therefore whether we should allow platforms to deploy attention-capture dark patterns against children without legal consequences.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And does IMDA have power to act on those assessments independently of content classification?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If so, will we commit to a timeline for doing so?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Two, given the findings about TikTok's addictive design, has IMDA reviewed TikTok's compliance report with this in mind?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Both children and their parents deserve a framework that holds platforms accountable, not just for what they show, but how they are built.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And design, when left unchecked, becomes policy by default.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It constantly awaits further completion with access to more information.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Knowledge about the past is important in shaping how we think and act in the present in tangible ways.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: More credible and independently verifiable information is crucial when disinformation, misinformation, confusion and uncertainty arrive.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Recent access to the Albatross Files underscores that separation with Malaysia was by mutual agreement.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This makes it more possible to go beyond the historical narrative of trauma surrounding being kicked out in Singapore, as we look to advance ties with our closest neighbour.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Elsewhere, opening the Epstein files enabled some of the richest and most powerful people in the world being held to account for wrongdoing, and led to figures like Andrew Mountbatten Windsor and Peter Mandelson to be arrested.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Access and accountability are especially important when the concerned persons remain alive, regardless of whether an issue is particularly heinous or more mundane.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Minister Josephine Teo stated that when deciding on access to public archives, state agencies take into consideration, and I quote: "supporting research into our collective past while safeguarding sensitive information and complying with relevant confidentiality and other obligations".

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We should add timelines, holding state agencies and political authority to public account and avoiding confusion as well as misrepresentation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In a democracy, state action needs to be defensible to the public it serves, and from which it derives funding.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: MDDI acknowledged that it has observed multiple online accounts publishing such fabricated claims about Singapore's domestic politics.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: An MDDI spokesman quoted by Zaobao stated that public education measures and resources have been rolled out and urged the public to rely on official sources and refrain from sharing unverified content.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I welcome this response, but I wonder if these measures are sufficient.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Enforcement tools like POFMA alone also cannot inoculate society against misinformation.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: We need a population equipped to question, verify and critically assess what they see online.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Will we expand community-based workshops, school curricula and public campaigns that teach citizens practical verification steps, such as checking original footage, examining sources, and consulting authoritative channels?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Can we leverage AI itself to help filter and flag suspicious content at scale?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: If AI lowers the cost of deception to $1 per video, then the cost of inaction may be far higher.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: How will our national AI strategy ensure that Singaporeans are empowered to discern fact from fiction in an increasingly polluted information ecosystem?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: For decades, the official narrative surrounding Singapore's independence was that we were abruptly and unilaterally expelled from Malaysia by the Federal Government.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: That story has shaped how generations of Singaporeans understand our nation's founding.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Yet, the Albatross File departs from the prevailing narrative.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The documents reveal that after the racial riots in July 1964, confidential talks had already commenced between the PAP and Malaysia's Alliance Party, regarding possible constitutional rearrangements within Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: This revelation does not diminish our history, it shows that history is often more complex than we think and enriches our understanding of history.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: But why did this historically significant recourse take so long to come to light?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: And how many other important records remain inaccessible?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party (WP) has long called for a freedom of Information Act, most recently in our General Election 2025 manifesto.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: This call is grounded in a simple principle – we trust Singaporeans with the information necessary to hold the Government accountable.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Citizens should be empowered under a Freedom of Information Act to make requests for, and given access to, information from public agencies at the level of detail that is requested.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Without a Freedom of Information Act and a framework for automatically declassifying record after 25 years, the Government would not be compelled to review and release information, and foundational truth risks remaining buried, indefinitely.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Facts and declassified documents can be cherry-picked to support a curated narrative.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: This is not what we want for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: A Freedom of Information Act and automatic declassification would shift the burden of proof from citizens to the Government.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The Government must justify why secrecy is needed, instead of citizens justifying curiosity.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: This empowers historians, journalists, civil society and ordinary Singaporeans to scrutinise decisions made in their name.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: A mature nation does not fear its own archives.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I believe that what the WP has proposed would strengthen our national identity rather than weaken it.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: We build a genuine national identity when it is grounded in facts, even when these facts are complex or uncomfortable.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: If we truly believe in accountable governance and informed citizenry, then it is time to enshrine the public's right to know, in law.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Christopher de Souza, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In this regard, I wish to place on record my strong support for the recent exhibition on the Albatross File and the team of officers behind it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The exhibition does excellent work in bringing into sharp focus the circumstances of independent Singapore's birth, the pressures of the time – 1963 to 1965 – and the difficult trade-offs faced by our leaders.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Understanding this history is not an academic exercise.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It shows how decisions were made firmly on principle, but tempered by deep pragmatism.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Faced with existential uncertainty, our Pioneers dug in, made hard choices and built a nation against the odds.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These decisions made in the crucible of crises, shaped the DNA of independent Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The pandemic was, after all, a recent and defining moment in Singapore's post-independent history.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Those late-night decisions, vaccine procurement choices, protecting lives and livelihoods, and the multiple debates we had in this House, between 2020 and 2022, and resuscitating Singapore Airlines.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It was a crisis of a generation and we prevailed together.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Decisions made in past crises shaped the DNA of a nation, and provide the ballast and compass for Singapore's future.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Lessons learned from them in more exhibitions, such as that on the COVID-19 crisis.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It can consume and summarise vast bodies of knowledge, but ultimately, AI is a tool.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It cannot be allowed to be the master.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thus, as we embrace AI, we must do so with discernment.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should use it to the extent that it facilitates decision-making, but it cannot be allowed to usurp our decision-making.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Innovation cannot come at the expense of trespassing on some existing IP rights.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And here, Sir, allow me to declare that I am a partner in a private law firm, practising IP law and advising on AI law.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In my view, there must be clear out-of-bound markers, no deepfakes, no deepfake pornography, no scams, no deception, no misrepresentation and no trespass on certain protected IP.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If Singapore can be an engine for AI adoption while retaining its status as a trusted IP hub, we would have struck the right balance.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In short, to discerningly balance AI's benefits without atrophying the human mind, we must ensure that AI remains the tool, not the master.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Mr Chairman, the Government has committed a large amount of money to support industries in their AI transformation.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: In this context, I am concerned about how today's fresh graduates are already being impacted, and the long-term compounding implications this has on our national talent pipeline.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: As Members from both sides of the House have spoken about this problem, I will not belabour the point further.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Today, I would like to provide a proposal which I hope the Government will consider.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: First, at the minimum, companies should be required to submit a structured declaration detailing how their AI transformation efforts are expected to impact HR decisions, particularly for entry-level roles.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: How many such roles will be eliminated or redesigned, and what career development support will be made available to affected employees?

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: This declaration will serve two purposes – to prompt companies to consider shaping their transformation efforts to protect their own talent pipeline and provide the Government with important insights on how entry-level roles may be impacted qualitatively and quantitatively across industries.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: To keep compliance manageable for SMEs, this second condition could be made mandatory only for companies above a particular threshold.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: To operationalise this, the National AI Council could coordinate with relevant agencies and consult the industry.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: For example, MDDI could take the lead in verifying companies' compliance with the conditions.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: In turn, only companies who receive this verification may submit Enterprise Innovation Scheme claims related to AI expenditures.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, conditions are already in place for some subsidy schemes.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The Productivity Solutions Grant already requires companies to submit a description of the overall impact of their proposed solution and specify the expected productivity gains before the grant application is reviewed and approved.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: To conclude, the entry level jobs of today shape the industry leaders of tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Let us ensure that our AI transformation amplifies, rather than erodes the career opportunities that our young graduates have worked hard to earn.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, Budget 2026 rightly places AI and automation at the centre of enterprise transformation.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: But if we want broad-based adoption, clarity and commercial realism matter as much as funding.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Many SMEs are not short of ambition, they are short of certainty.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Uncertainty about what qualifies as AI or automation expenditure; how bundled digital costs are treated; how robotics hardware and software layers are classified; and what documentation withstands audit scrutiny?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In a tight cashflow environment, hesitation becomes inaction.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Spending labelled as AI without measurable productivity impact.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Second, under-adoption, with firms delaying genuine transformation due to compliance risk.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Integration, deployment, robotics installation and workflow redesign costs are immediate.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If we want transformation beyond leading enterprises, the model must be simple – de-risk early, reward outcomes strongly.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It would subsidise results – measurable improvements in output per worker, value-add per employee or cost efficiencies.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Such a model aligns public spending with real productivity gains and gives SMEs the confidence to commit.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We must also be careful about how we frame AI nationally.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Public discourse often centres on GenAI and digital tools.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: But in labour-intensive sectors – logistics, F&B, facilities management, manufacturing – robotics and advanced automation may deliver more immediate productivity gains.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: MDDI plays a critical role in shaping that narrative.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It is robotics, process redesign and job redesign.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: From an SME's perspective, the landscape can feel fragmented.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In a structurally tight labour market, productivity is existential.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Transformation must therefore be: clear in definition; coherent in communication; and commercially rational in incentive design.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If we get this right – de-risk early and reward real outcomes decisively – we can achieve economy-wide transformation, not isolated pilot processes.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Mr Chairman, in my work with stroke survivors, we use brain imaging and machine learning to understand how the brain reorganises after injury.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A single scan can produce thousands of images.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Algorithms help us detect patterns we would otherwise miss.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But no responsible scientist relies on a model blindly.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We validate it rigorously, test for bias and examine when it breaks, because a wrong conclusion does not stay in a journal.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As Singapore accelerates our AI ambitions, we should bring that same discipline to national deployment.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is the right posture: AI – not as a buzzword, but as an economic strategy.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To make AI translate into growth that Singaporeans can feel, three disciplines matter.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The jump from "trying tools" to "redesigning work" is where productivity is won.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We should help firms, especially SMEs, cross that gap with mission-linked sector playbooks, reference workflows and practical benchmarks.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: AI must generate enterprise value, not just technological activity.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In a fragmented world, Singapore's brand is that we are a place where serious systems run reliably.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As AI systems move from assisting decisions to shaping outcomes, assurance cannot be informal.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For high-impact deployments, institutionalising testing, explainability where needed and independent review where appropriate will strengthen confidence without stifling innovation.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We will need people fluent in both domain and data, professionals who understand context, model limits and risk.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The future workforce must be fluent in both code and context.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If we build value, trust, and bilingual talent, Singapore will not merely adopt AI.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We will shape how it is deployed and ensure that our growth is resilient and inclusive.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I welcome the Minister's reflections on how MDDI will drive these disciplines through the National AI Council and the AI Missions.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Cassandra Lee, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Mr Chairman, this AI transformation must be managed carefully because it brings anxiety to many.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: From my conversations with youths, two concerns have been repeatedly raised.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: On displacement, young professionals and youths preparing for their first jobs are concerned that their jobs will be displaced by AI.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Youths I have spoken to have shared that they are worried that they cannot keep up with the pace at which AI is evolving.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: And as AI make some tasks redundant, their jobs may also be made redundant.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This applies to both youths looking to enter the workforce and those already in the workforce.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Despite being digital natives, professionals and even technology professionals, they are nervous that it would be difficult to get ahead of the AI curve.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Many of those in the workforce are willing to upskill but they are time-poor.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: They need flexibility in training, employer support and buy-in and clear outcomes from each course that they take.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Employers, in turn, ask for confidence and assurance that training translates into productivity.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: So, the question is not what to train, but how to make training work in practice.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I support the Government's plans to explore how it can broaden the TeSA programme to help all young Singaporean workers continue to stay relevant.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: On right-sizing AI adoption, AI adoption will not be one-size-fits-all.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Different firms in different sectors face different constraints.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: As we all know, SMEs employ the majority of our workforce, with nearly half in small and micro enterprises.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But many SMEs face real constraints: cashflow, uncertainty of returns, manpower and implementation capacity.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Not just funding, but end-to-end support to help enterprises adopt, integrate, scale AI in their core processes, redesign legacy systems and tailor solutions to different business needs.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: These uneven application of AI adoption heighten uncertainty amongst youths as to job security and progression.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: For example, will the Ministry facilitate the provision of shared solutions or proven use cases jointly developed with trade associations and Institutes of Higher Learning?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The newly announced Champions of AI programme will go some way to support the integration of AI into business processes.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I understand that MDDI is looking at supporting our libraries with renewed possibilities.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Henry Kwek, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Mr Chairman, AI-centric IT development is no longer theoretical.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In Silicon Valley, leading AI firms and hyperscalers have moved beyond traditional software development.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Frameworks now include intention-based engineering, vibe coding and agentic development.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: More top programmers are publicly saying they no longer code traditionally.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It has integral to design, coding, testing and continuous improvement.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It could be structural inertia within IT services firms and if they do not adopt these new paradigms quickly, our ambitions remain on paper.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Should we leverage on these partnerships not just for enterprise development, but also to transform how our IT companies build software?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We mandated Building Information Modelling adoption in construction procurement, and it transformed that industry.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And beyond the tech sector, how can we encourage both our multinational companies (MNCs) and SMEs to embrace AI in their own operations?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Mr Chairman, our Public Service Media companies – Mediacorp, Zaobao, CNA, Business Times – are not just Singapore's truth infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In an age of AI-generated disinformation, like what some of our Members talked about earlier, they stand between our people and in a manipulated information environment.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Unlike commercial outlets, our Public Service Media also carries nation-building obligations, serving all communities fairly, building social cohesiveness and upholding our national interest.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Even reputable international outlets like the Washington Post have to resort to dramatic cuts.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Can MDDI outline its vision for keeping our national media compelling, relevant and thriving?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We should not underestimate what we already have.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Zaobao is already one of the most respected Chinese-language outlet globally.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And with the strategic investment, The Business Times could become the Financial Times of Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Our Public Service Media a key source of our soft power.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Our media must also stay relevant for all Singaporeans, starting with our students.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Countries like Australia and the UK have ensured that public service content remains prominent and easily discoverable on connected television platforms.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Can we do the same, so that the quality of local content is not buried by algorithms favouring overseas programming?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Our Public Service Media companies are our national assets.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I hope MDDI can share how it plans to secure our future.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I notice I have 18 more seconds, so I want to add in a final point.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I noted we are asking MDDI to do a lot of cybersecurity, national Public Service Media on IT services and AI development.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Chairman, we are an open society, physically and virtually.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Information pours in from every direction and discerning truth has never been harder.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: A resident of mine whom I met during a block visit in January believed the story so wholeheartedly that I found it hard to dissuade him.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: They corrode mutual trust, weaken social cohesion and create fertile ground for scams.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Our Public Service Media plays a central role in preserving factual public discourse and remains the go-to source of truth for important issues by our citizens.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: First, how will the Government support and strengthen our Public Service Media so it can more effectively in countering fake news and misinformation in an increasingly noisy information environment?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: This means funding, talent development, editorial independence and technical capability to verify rapidly and at scale.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Second, what concrete steps will be taken to ensure Public Service Media content remains high quality and highly accessible, across languages, platforms and demographics, so that credible information reaches every community before falsehoods do?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Likewise, how will we ensure genuine and verified Singapore narratives reach international audiences, both to protect our reputation from falsehoods and to project our voice on matters of global significance?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Third, will the Government equip our Public Service Media and our public agencies with advanced tools, including responsibly governed AI to detect, attribute and counter disinformation?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Put simply, can we use AI to fight AI, with safeguards to avoid overreach, bias or erosion of privacy?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: In an age when technology amplifies both benefit and risk, we must ensure our public information architecture is robust, trusted and adaptive.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: As Singapore embraces AI as a strategic necessity for our development, we must protect the long‑term interests of our people even as we harness its power.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Much of the public conversation today veers toward doom‑laden predictions of AI "taking over" jobs and society.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: We can choose how AI is designed, governed and deployed.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: That choice demands strong national leadership to chart practical governance pathways and sustained international cooperation to agree what ought not to be delegated to machines.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Interoperable standards and certification, robust procurement and audit requirements, independent oversight and investments in public literacy and workforce reskilling so that citizens can exercise meaningful agency.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Jessica Tan, please take your three cuts together.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, Budget 2026 underscores an important priority, keeping Singaporeans safe from scams and online harms.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Digital safety today is no longer just about avoiding suspicious links.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: AI has changed the way scams and online threats work.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The tools used to deceive people are more sophisticated, more personal and harder to detect, even for those who are usually confident online.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We now see AI‑generated deepfakes that could sound exactly like a family member or friend with uncanny accuracy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Hyper‑personalised scams tailor messages to a person's habits, vulnerabilities and online behaviour.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Misinformation spread faster at a scale that outpace fact‑checking.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And these risks fall disproportionately on seniors, youth, lower‑income families, and those who may not have the digital confidence to tell what is real and what is AI-generated.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To keep Singaporeans safe, we now must move from "digital safety" to AI risk resilience, equipping people with practical skills, trusted tools and strong community support.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Four, leveraging the base of Digital Ambassadors, develop a network of community-based digital safety ambassadors focused on AI risks in senior activity centres, schools and social service settings.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, digital safety tools are about protecting trust, protecting families and ensuring every Singaporean, regardless of age or background, feels confident and safe in an AI-driven world.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, this year's Budget rightly emphasises the importance of responsible AI.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Singapore has already built strong foundations – from the Model AI Governance Framework to AI Verify – and sector‑specific guidelines in finance and healthcare.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These are real strengths, and they show our commitment to safe and trustworthy innovation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But as AI becomes part of everyday decisions that affect people's lives, Singaporeans now need more clarity, more consistency and more accountability.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Today, AI is already used in hiring, credit assessment, insurance underwriting and even public sector processes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Many Singaporeans may not even know when AI is involved.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Without regular checks, these systems can unintentionally reinforce or amplify bias.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: At the same time, we know that modern AI, especially frontier models, is complex and often proprietary.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While transparency and independent evaluation sound simple, the reality is more challenging.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Singapore's existing frameworks recognise this, but the pace of deployment means we need to strengthen our approach in a practical and proportionate way.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Not all AI systems can carry the same level of risk.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: A chatbot answering Frequently Asked Questions is not the same as an algorithm screening job applicants, assessing creditworthiness or supporting medical decisions.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And transparency does not mean revealing source code.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It simply means explaining what the system does, what risks it carries and what safeguards are in place.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Independent audits should only be required where the potential harm is significant.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The European Union already mandates audits for high‑risk systems.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: US regulators require audits in finance and healthcare.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The United Kingdom (UK) is strengthening evaluation requirements for frontier models.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Singapore should stay ahead, but in a way that fits our context and supports innovation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: A risk‑based approach allows us to protect Singaporeans while keeping compliance practical.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This ensures we do not overburden SMEs or slow innovation while still giving Singaporeans confidence that AI is being used responsibly.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: My recommendation is for the Government to co-develop practical guidance, sandboxes and sector‑specific standards with industry, building on strong foundations we already have.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This turns responsible AI into a shared national capability and not just a regulatory obligation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, Budget 2026 gives Singapore's AI push real momentum.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Will AI make daily work easier, more productive and more meaningful for our people?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Compute is costly, data is fragmented, governance feels complex and workers worry about job impact.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If we do not address these realities, AI will benefit only a few.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is how trusted AI becomes a catalyst, not a compliance burden.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Champions of AI programme is promising, but AI adoption is about more than tools.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is about preparing data, redesigning workflows and helping workers feel confident.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The workforce transformation roadmaps must go beyond broad skills.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, when we combine practical support, clear AI trust guidance, empowered workers, strong cybersecurity and a vibrant local ecosystem, AI becomes a real productivity tool and boost for our enterprises – and a real competitive advantage for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Members for their cuts.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Chairman, in the blink of an eye, tomorrow will be Chap Goh Meh.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Before Chinese New Year, I asked my mother if she wanted me to accompany her to buy new clothes, but the 83-year-old said, "No need!

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I have already found the clothes I like online and placed an order." I was afraid that she might be scammed, so I asked her how she knew that the seller was reliable.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: She confidently replied, "I will only pay after I receive the goods and am satisfied with them." On the day of our reunion dinner, she excitedly showed me her new clothes, and only then did I feel reassured.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, digital technology has brought a lot of conveniences to our lives and created new opportunities for our businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, it has also exposed us to unprecedented risks and dangers.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Some Singaporeans worry that they cannot keep up with the pace of this AI era.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I have also felt the same way before.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, as the Prime Minister said, we cannot stand still out of fear of AI.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As the saying goes, "Like a boat going against the current, you must move forward; otherwise, you will fall behind." Other countries have developed their AI initiatives.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: If we do not act fast enough, plan broadly enough, or establish our foundations deeply enough, we will inevitably fall behind.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The key is that our goals must be clear, and our measures effective.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In this AI era, how can we ensure that Singaporeans are not left behind and help SMEs maintain their competitive advantage?

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is a core issue that we are closely monitoring.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Just like my mother – she is not a digital expert, but with appropriate help, she too can shop online safely.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We do not need to force ourselves to become AI masters, because not everyone can master AI to the same degree; the ways in which they benefit from it will also differ.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: More importantly, Singapore must remain confident so that we can move steadily ahead in this AI era.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In this year's COS debate, MDDI will propose various initiatives in this direction and ensure that Singaporeans can not only keep up but also benefit. : Mr Chairman, AI has taken centre stage at this year's Budget and COS debates.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Members have shared optimism about opportunities and anxiety over impacts on our jobs, creativity and autonomy.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Sharael Taha asked a strategic question about Singapore's unique positioning in AI.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We are fortunate that international counterparts recognise our ability to respond holistically across industries, enterprises and the workforce through a range of enablers – from R&D and infrastructure to safety and governance.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: On the global stage, Singapore is frequently at the table.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our progressive, thoughtful approach to AI makes us a credible partner and useful reference point.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This has made it possible to aim higher.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Prime Minister Wong, Deputy Prime Minister Gan and MTI colleagues outlined plans to grow AI champions and pursue national AI Missions.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Later, Ministry of Manpower (MOM) and MOE colleagues will discuss how we empower the present and future workforce to make the most of AI.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I will focus on what this means for the broader base of our businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In gist, we want to take full advantage of AI's ability to be democratised, or to put it more simply, for its benefits to spread widely because solutions once too expensive or complex are more accessible.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But if AI follows the same path as previous technology waves, only a small group of companies at the frontier will get ahead and pull away from the pack.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The long tail of smaller and often less-resourced businesses take much longer.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Yet collectively, they employ most of our workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: When they fall behind, more than GDP is at risk.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We want to encourage those who have not started to take the first step and help those already using AI move beyond basic applications.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will create a sizable pool of early adopters.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They can be multipliers in the community, sharing their experiences and knowledge through the intermediaries that Ms Denise Phua asked the Prime Minister about.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Take Durian Memories for example, a single store seller in Ang Mo Kio.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They did not have the luxury of dedicating a team member to handle customer enquiries.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Unsurprisingly, they lost sales when hungry durian lovers were not attended to.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But Durian Memories tackled this challenge by implementing an AI-enabled customer relationship management system with a chatbot that automatically answers customer queries.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will expand the range of AI-enabled solutions with grant support to meet different business needs.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: More SMEs can then access these pre-approved, cost-effective and market-proven tools to integrate AI readily and affordably.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Like Mr Pritam Singh and Mr Muhaimin, we want these solutions to be transformative yet human-centred.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the same time, Mr Mark Lee worries about AI washing.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will put safeguards in place for grants and incentives whilst trying at the same time to not make the rules too onerous.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Some enterprises are ready to do more with AI.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They are a talented team of multimedia creators who improve film visuals and sound.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Unknown to most of us, sound effects are still added manually to films, often taking four to eight weeks.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This innovation allowed the company to not only save costs but create a potential new income stream.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It has opened up opportunities for both the business and their employees.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We want more success stories like Mocha Chai.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But as pointed out by Ms Jessica Tan, Mr Mark Lee and Mr Sharael Taha, more sophisticated uses of AI require multiple factors to succeed.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We also thank Mr Andre Low, Mr Dennis Tan and Mr Fadli Fawzi as well as Mr Sharael Taha for recognising the need to plan ahead, as the Government has done, to manage the energy impact of widespread AI use.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We are judicious in how we expand digital infrastructure.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: When allocating new data centres, we assess how well they use low-carbon energy sources.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We are introducing new sustainability requirements to improve the energy efficiency of older data centres.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: And through the National AI Research and Development plan, we will support public research in resource-efficient AI to better understand our options.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As more businesses adopt AI, there is also opportunity to uplift the workforce and help them stay relevant, whether at the entry level or at later stages of their careers.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Beyond the Prime Minister's commitments and MOM’s plans, I want to assure Members like Mr Abdul Muhaimin, Ms Cassandra Lee and Dr Choo Pei Ling that MDDI is focused squarely on this.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We know that PMEs and knowledge workers feel the pressure more acutely.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But many have found ways to be more effective with AI’s help.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Take Geraldine Lau, an audit professional who has been with KPMG for 27 years.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For each audit, Geraldine pores through reams of documents to assess risk.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With employer-provided training, she created an AI agent that automatically consolidates key information from company announcements for audit reviews.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The AI agent organises information more quickly than Geraldine can, but her domain knowledge is key to ensuring it looks in the right places.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With hours of manual work saved, she can now focus on deeper risk assessments and applying her human abilities – wisdom, calibration and professional judgement – to more complex work.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Geraldine and many PMEs are showing that AI know-how, domain expertise and human touch are a powerful combination.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Not all of us can be AI engineers.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But we can be “bilingual” in AI in our own areas of expertise and to solve problems in our domains.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They will be pathfinders for meaningful AI upskilling, for others to emulate.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our initial focus will be on professions that are highly exposed to AI and serve multiple industries.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will start with the accountancy and legal professions, and extend our reach to other fields such as HR.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As Mr Henry Kwek noted, AI is also transforming the tech sector – many people can now write code and build prototypes with the help of AI.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will therefore enhance the TeSA offerings to help tech workers move up the value chain, from writing code, to orchestrating end-to-end systems powered by AI agents.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With AI evolving quickly, our governance must also keep pace.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We agree with Ms Jessica Tan and Dr Choo Pei Ling on risk-based, practical AI governance.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Like Mr Christopher de Souza, we believe AI should not replace the discerning human mind.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We are the first government worldwide to introduce such guidelines.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For high-risk, high-impact systems like frontier models, we will progressively strengthen safeguards.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, what we do locally is not enough, a point noted by Ms Tin Pei Ling.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The most advanced AI models are developed in only a handful of countries, but their cooperation on AI safety is not deep.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In recent years, Singapore has hosted major AI conferences to promote international cooperation.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Last year, we organised the Singapore Conference on AI: International Scientific Exchange on AI Safety.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The exchange brought together world-class thinkers across research, government and civil society, resulting in the Singapore Consensus on global AI safety research priorities.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Recently, at the India AI Impact Summit, I shared that Singapore will host the second edition of the International Scientific Exchange to update the Singapore Consensus.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Despite the challenges, we will continue contributing meaningfully to the international discourse on AI safety.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Members are understandably concerned about whether our critical infrastructure is sufficiently protected against malicious threat actors, especially state-sponsored ones.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: On the diplomatic front, Singapore recently concluded our chairmanship of the Second UN Open-Ended Working Group on security of and in the use of info-comm technologies.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Realistically, state-sponsored threat actors are par for the course.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is nonetheless important to forge international consensus on what constitutes responsible state behaviour in cyberspace.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We must, however, not expect these efforts to be a substitute for stronger cyber defense capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In this regard, CSA will focus on three key areas.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Senior Minister of State Tan Kiat How will say more about these efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Another risk we face is the spread of disinformation and misinformation, fueled by technologies like AI.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As a diverse society, we are particularly vulnerable to online falsehoods that erode trust in our society and institutions.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Fortunately, we have been strengthening our libraries and archives.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They help to nurture a discerning population by cultivating reading habits and information literacy.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Minister of State Rahayu will share more later.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our Public Service Media entities too, are important in maintaining trust in our infospace.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They remain highly trusted by the public, more so than reputable international and online media outlets.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Consequently, our Public Service Media entities have become indispensable in countering misinformation.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: MDDI will therefore continue working closely with our Public Service Media entities to maintain their reach and strengthen their fact-checking capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Government agencies have also collaborated with The Straits Times on the AskST series to address misinformation.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Henry Kwek asked about efforts to help Public Service Media remain relevant, discoverable and financially viable as audience attention and advertising shift towards digital platforms.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Besides delivering timely and credible news, our Public Service Media entities produce content that strengthens our sense of identity as one people.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They also play a role in cultivating news literacy among our young, through regular student publications and school competitions.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Given the critical role of our Public Service Media, MDDI will support efforts to keep public service media content visible and easily discoverable.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We are studying approaches in other countries and will consult the industry to ensure that initiatives are implemented reasonably and effectively.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Government will continue investing in our Public Service Media entities, helping them develop new capabilities as the media landscape evolves.

speaker: The Minister for Digital Development and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: By accelerating AI adoption, strengthening technology governance, and building discernment among our people, we are positioning Singaporeans to seize the opportunities and make progress together.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: I agree with Mr Vikram Nair’s cut to the Ministry of Home Affairs that threat actors, especially APTs, will only get more sophisticated.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Mr Sharael Taha asked about the Government’s plan to protect our CII.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: CII owners must take responsibility of the systems they own and operate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: At this COS, I will speak about MDDI’s plans to first, update the cybersecurity standards and obligations; second, level up our CII owners; and third, strengthen capabilities in our cybersecurity workforce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Today, our CII owners are held to higher standards and stringent obligations are imposed on their critical systems or CII systems.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: This was a calibrated approach to balance national security needs and business costs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We have observed that threat actors are also targeting non-CII systems because they may be less secured and can be entry points into CII systems.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We are mindful not to impose unnecessary costs on CII owners, and will continue to take a risk-based, calibrated and pragmatic approach.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Sector Leads may introduce additional sector-specific obligations that are adapted for their sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: IMDA intends to provide guidance for areas such as managing virtualisation of infrastructure and credential management.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We expect CII owners to comply with these requirements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: CII owners currently engage third parties to conduct audits and regular penetration testings to verify their robustness of their defences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: These reports are then submitted to CSA for review.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: In addition to relying on such third party reports, CSA wants to ensure that the security controls implemented by CII owners are not only tested and validated during audits but continuously strengthened.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: One way to do so will be to partner CII owners to do on-site reviews.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: CSA is currently discussing with the Sector Leads on the implementation plan.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We will reach out to the identified CII owners when ready.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We need our sectors and our CII owners to do their part to defend their systems, consistently every day.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Over the last year, I have visited the CII sectors, taking time to speak with the sector leads and the key CII owners.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Our Sector Leads and CII owners understand that the threat landscape has evolved and appreciate what is at stake.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: However, they shared with me that most CII owners are private companies whose business is in the delivery of essential services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Yet, they are up against the best-in-class, state-backed cyber threat actors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: One of the Chief Information Security Officers told me that it is like he is bringing a knife to a gun fight.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: As I said, cybersecurity is a collective effort.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Therefore, the Government will lean in to help CII owners to strengthen their defences and better respond to incidents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Typically, national security is the exclusive domain of governments, such as developing cutting-edge technological systems and training skilled operators to deal with various threat scenarios.
